title: Day 40 · Week 5, Day 5 — Protocol: the first-visit question list — what the hour contains, the seven screens behind it, and the eight questions to bring in writing
summary: The second Protocol episode, promised on Day 39. Your baby is 3–5 mm at Carnegie stage 12, the caudal neuropore sealing and the limb buds distinct. The first prenatal visit is late by design: the NHS booking appointment at 8–12 weeks takes about an hour, NICE NG201 offers it by 10+0 weeks and plans 10 visits for a first pregnancy and 7 after that, the US schedule runs monthly to 28 weeks and lands at 12–14 visits, and WHO's 2016 minimum is 8 contacts. What the count buys: Cochrane 2015 (7 trials, >60,000 women) found 14% higher perinatal mortality with reduced visits, entirely from low-income trials with under five visits; in high-income settings neither fewer visits nor hybrid video schedules changed outcomes (Balk 2022), which is why ACOG's 2025 Clinical Consensus 8 now tailors the schedule and accepts telehealth. The hour itself: the history including both parents' family history, three measurements, and the seven screens with their numbers — Rh typing (USPSTF A; the father's blood type matters if she is Rh-negative), full blood count, urine culture (2–10% bacteriuria; treatment cuts pyelonephritis 76%), hepatitis B (A; 3.8% transmission untreated, under 1% with birth prophylaxis), HIV (A; 9–67% untreated vs under 1–3% on treatment), syphilis (A, 2025; 3,882 congenital cases in 2023 vs 334 in 2012, ~90% preventable), rubella, hepatitis C, haemoglobinopathies and STI cultures — then the four NICE risk assessments, including the pre-eclampsia checklist that decides whether aspirin 81 mg starts at 12 weeks (RR 0.85; baseline 4%, high risk ≥8%), the mental-health questions and the domestic-abuse question asked with the partner out of the room. Why to write it down: 40–80% of medical information is forgotten immediately and half of the rest is wrong (Kessels 2003); question lists before consultations raise question-asking and satisfaction in 33 RCTs of 8,244 patients (Kinnersley, Cochrane 2007). Then the eight questions, in the order the visit runs, each anchored to Days 28–39: dating, the scan, the screening menu including carrier screening and the father's family history, the medication and supplement audit, the nausea plan, the risk flags (aspirin, Rh), logistics and travel, and screening for both parents. And how to run the room: who writes, recording, teach-back, the notes, and whose appointment it is.
action: Tonight, write the eight questions on one sheet in your own handwriting, with space under each for the answer, and put it in the pregnancy file: (1) our due date from her LMP and cycle length, and will the scan change it; (2) when is the first scan, what for, transvaginal?; (3) which bloods today and how we get results, plus which chromosomal screening is offered and when, and whether carrier screening should be done now; (4) the medication and supplement audit — bring the bottles and the label photo; (5) the nausea plan — B6, dose, doxylamine, call thresholds; (6) the risk flags — aspirin from 12 weeks, Rh status and whether my blood type matters; (7) how many visits, which by video, the after-hours number, and the booked trip; (8) will both of us be screened for depression. On the back, write your own family history and ancestry and ask your parents tomorrow about anything you're unsure of; then find out your blood type.
